name: Abū Muḥammad al-Qāsim ibn ʿAlī al-Ḥarīrī al-Baṣrī
summary: The author of the Maqāmāt, the most admired book of Arabic prose, who also put grammar into verse in Mulḥat al-iʿrāb and listed the mistakes of the learned in Durrat al-ghawwāṣ.
bio: Al-Ḥarīrī was born near Basra in 446/1054 and lived there all his life, a man of means and an official of the Saljūq administration. His fifty Maqāmāt, tales of a silver-tongued vagabond in rhymed prose, were read and commented on across the Islamic world and copied with famous illustrations.

In grammar he wrote Mulḥat al-iʿrāb, a poem of some three hundred and seventy verses that sets out naḥw for beginners, with his own commentary; it was a school text for centuries, before the Alfiyya. His Durrat al-ghawwāṣ fī awhām al-khawāṣṣ collects the mistakes of educated people, with the correct forms. He died in Basra in 516/1122.
